catalysts.description: NVIDIA continues to report record data-center revenue and strong AI demand commentary, signaling that accelerator demand remains the central system driver.
Amazon disclosed about $200 billion of expected 2026 capex, with explicit AI and data-center investment emphasis, supporting a large downstream demand pulse.
Microsoft's latest earnings materials describe AI-driven cloud strength, suggesting continued Azure demand for AI infrastructure and services.
Arista's 2025 and early 2026 results show continued AI networking momentum and double-digit revenue growth, supporting the thesis that cluster networking remains a live bottleneck layer.
Vertiv's backlog, book-to-bill, and organic order growth point to sustained AI data-center power and cooling demand, indicating that physical infrastructure remains a bottleneck.
Hyperscaler announcements around additional NVIDIA GPU deployments and broader AI chip adoption imply ongoing customer pull-through for compute and networking supply.

evidence.claim: NVIDIA reported record third-quarter fiscal 2026 revenue of $57.0 billion and record data-center revenue of $51.2 billion, with management saying cloud GPUs are sold out and compute demand keeps accelerating.
evidence.source_title: NVIDIA Announces Financial Results for Third Quarter Fiscal 2026

evidence.claim: NVIDIA reported fourth-quarter fiscal 2025 revenue of $39.3 billion and record data-center revenue of $35.6 billion, showing the scale of AI accelerator demand before the next leg of growth.
evidence.source_title: NVIDIA Announces Financial Results for Fourth Quarter and Fiscal 2025

evidence.claim: Microsoft's FY25 Q4 earnings release said Azure surpassed $75 billion in revenue for the year and described strength from Microsoft Cloud and AI.

Amazon's Q1 2026 release said AWS revenue increased 28% year over year to $37.6 billion and that the company landed more than 2.1 million AI chips over the past 12 months while planning about 1 million+ NVIDIA GPUs starting in 2026.
Amazon's Q4 2025 release said the company expects to invest about $200 billion in capital expenditures across Amazon in 2026, explicitly citing AI as a major opportunity.
Arista reported Q4 and full-year 2025 results with revenue growth and explicitly positioned itself in large AI and data-center networking environments.
evidence.source_title: Arista Networks Reports Fourth Quarter and Year End 2025 Financial Results

evidence.claim: Vertiv said its fourth-quarter 2025 organic orders grew about 81% year over year, with backlog at $15.0 billion and demand particularly strong in AI infrastructure.
evidence.source_title: Vertiv Reports Strong Fourth Quarter with Organic Orders Growth of 252% and Diluted EPS Growth of 200%

evidence.claim: Vertiv announced OneCore, a prefabricated solution for AI, HPC, and high-density 5+ MW data centers, indicating physical infrastructure adaptation to AI density.
Vertiv announced intent to acquire PurgeRite to expand liquid-cooling services for data centers and next-generation thermal chains.
evidence.source_title: Vertiv Announces Intent to Acquire PurgeRite

evidence.claim: GE Vernova is exposed to the AI power bottleneck through grid, turbine, and electrification equipment, but the AI-specific revenue contribution is not yet quantified in this pass.

memory_update.text: For AI, the highest-priority layers remain accelerators, advanced packaging/foundry, networking, and data-center power/cooling; hyperscalers are the demand engines rather than the bottleneck themselves.
Power and thermal management are emerging as a real chokepoint because higher rack density and liquid-cooling requirements can slow deployment even when compute supply is available.
AI networking is a separate bottleneck from compute; large-cluster rollouts require switch fabrics and Ethernet gear that can gate deployment timing.
Hyperscaler capex guidance and AI chip deployment announcements remain the fastest-moving catalysts for this theme and should be checked every earnings cycle.
Memory/HBM, advanced packaging subcontractors, photonics, and test/inspection equipment are under-covered and should be searched next with primary-source evidence.

summary: AI demand is still being pulled by hyperscaler capex and model deployment, while the tightest near-term chokepoints appear to be compute supply, networking, data-center power/cooling, and grid/electrical buildout. The strongest current evidence is for NVIDIA, Amazon/AWS, Microsoft Azure, Arista, and Vertiv; the weakest part of the map remains memory/HBM, advanced packaging, photonics, and test/inspection, which should be searched next. This pass separates demand engines from bottleneck suppliers and flags where evidence is still mostly inference from earnings commentary and product announcements rather than hard capacity data.

supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Meta are the primary buyers of AI compute, networking, storage, and power infrastructure; their capex decisions determine downstream order flow.
Accelerators are the core scarce compute input for training and inference; shortages here ripple into systems, networking, and data-center deployment timing.
Leading-edge wafer supply and packaging capacity constrain how quickly AI accelerators can be manufactured and delivered.
High-speed Ethernet and switch fabrics are required to connect large GPU clusters; cluster scaling can be gated by networking rollout.
HBM and advanced memory are critical to accelerator performance and cluster availability; shortages can constrain shipment mix and system throughput.
AI density raises power, cooling, and rack-level thermal requirements; deployment can stall without electrical and liquid-cooling infrastructure.
Even if GPUs are available, sites need substation, distribution, and utility interconnect capacity; this can become a hard timing constraint.
Applications and agents create demand for inference tokens and cloud usage, but are usually less supply-constrained than infrastructure layers.
